name: Numbered perfumery / analogs

card.summary: Numbered perfumery lines sell fragrances identified by number or code that are made to smell like well-known designer or niche scents, giving people a way to wear a popular, well-liked scent as part of their grooming at a lower price.
card.note: Analogs usually differ from the originals in opening, longevity and complexity; skin sensitivity to fragrance ingredients applies as with any perfume.

quick.overview:
Numbered perfumery refers to fragrance houses and lines that label products with numbers or codes instead of evocative names, often so that each code corresponds to a known scent it is modeled on. These analogs, also called dupes, clones or inspired-by fragrances, let a person smell like a popular designer or niche perfume without paying its price. Scent is part of grooming and first impressions, so the payoff is smelling the way an expensive fragrance is meant to smell.

Independent write-ups describe three categories: clones that aim to replicate one fragrance, inspired-by scents that borrow its character, and similar scents that share notes. They report that almost none are identical to the target, with differences in the opening, longevity and complexity.
quick.how: People pick a fragrance they like from a designer or niche house, find an analog that reviewers describe as matching it, and wear it as they would any perfume. Some buy small sizes first. Prices in retail guides run roughly $15 to $60 for analogs against roughly $200 to $400 for the originals.
quick.risks: Perfume ingredients can irritate or trigger allergies in some people. Reviewers say analogs often last fewer hours on skin than the originals and may smell flatter as they dry down. Sellers of counterfeit bottles of the original brands are a separate issue from honestly labeled analogs.

lead: Numbered perfumery, also called analogs, is a way of selling fragrance in which a cheap, generic bottle carries a number or code instead of an evocative name, and the product is offered as an 'aroma in the direction of' a famous perfume or as a 'version' of it. Wikipedia's perfume article describes the practice under the Russian-language name 'nomernaya parfyumeriya' (numbered perfumery), known in countries of the former USSR, and says such products usually carry three-digit registered names such as #105 [2].

The appearance payoff is scent as part of grooming. Fragrance is part of how a person presents and is perceived, and an analog lets someone wear a recognizable, widely admired scent profile, of the kind associated with designer or niche houses, at a fraction of the original price. Retail guides to the wider 'dupe' category divide such products into clones that aim to copy a specific fragrance, inspired-by scents that borrow its general character, and similar scents that share notes [1].

The practice sits at the edge of a long-running legal debate about whether a scent can be owned. Formulas of commercial perfumes are held as trade secrets, courts in different countries have disagreed on whether a perfume can be protected by copyright, and a 2009 European Court of Justice ruling involving a 'smell-alike' comparison list favored the brand owner [2][4].

chain: Pick a scent associated with a popular fragrance
Wear a numbered analog of it
Smell like a well-regarded fragrance at lower cost
angle.text: The analog delivers a similar scent directly on skin. Reviewers say it can come close but generally differs in opening, longevity and development [1].

infobox: Numbers or codes (often three digits, e.g. #105) instead of names [2]
Generic bottle; labeled as 'in the direction of' or a 'version' of a known perfume [2]
Eau de parfum about 15-20%, extrait about 15-30% [2]
Varies by country; formula copyright unsettled in US and divided in Europe [2]

paras: According to Wikipedia, a company that owns perfume-compounding equipment uses one inexpensive bottle style and a numeric registered name, and states on the label that the contents smell in the direction of a known perfume or are a version of it [2]. Alcohol-based versions may carry a harsh alcohol note, and some makers sell propylene glycol or dipropylene glycol 'perfume oils' in 50 ml roller bottles; the article cites Fidji by Guy Laroche as an example of a scent analogs imitate, and reports bulk online purchases bringing a 100 ml bottle to roughly 6 euros [2].

A buyer's guide on Fragplace, written about the wider dupe market, says almost no dupe smells identical to its target, that differences typically show in the first 15 to 30 minutes where cheaper versions often use synthetics, and in longevity and complexity [1]. Named examples in that guide include alternatives to Baccarat Rouge 540, Santal 33 and Creed Aventus, such as Club de Nuit Intense Man, priced around $25 against roughly $380 for the original [1].

Numbers have a long history in perfume naming. Chanel No. 5 takes its name from a trial of numbered sample vials prepared by perfumer Ernest Beaux in 1920, from which Coco Chanel chose the fifth; the perfume launched on 5 May 1921 [3]. Modern numbered analogs use the number differently, as a code for an imitation rather than a brand's chosen name [2].

Imitating popular scents is also linked to the history of synthetic aroma compounds. Wikipedia notes that modern perfumery began in the late 19th century with synthesis of compounds such as vanillin and coumarin, that a handful of companies (Givaudan, IFF, Firmenich, Robertet, Takasago, Symrise) produce most synthetic aromatics, and that synthetics are more consistent than naturals [2]. Because the accords of a famous perfume are built from available aroma chemicals, other makers can aim at similar profiles [1][2].

The Fragplace guide reports that dupes often last less time than originals, giving 8 or more hours for a luxury fragrance against 4 to 6 for a dupe, while some budget options are praised for projection [1]. It also says a bottle priced around $3 per 100 ml is likely synthetic oil in alcohol [1]. Wikipedia adds that concentration terms are imprecise because houses define them differently, and that the same product name can have different compositions at different concentrations [2].

Wikipedia states that exact formulas of commercial perfumes are kept as trade secrets, and that it is doubtful whether perfumes qualify as copyright subject matter in the United States, where no court has addressed the question. In the Netherlands the Supreme Court granted copyright to Lancome's Tresor in Lancome v. Kecofa (2006), while the French Supreme Court twice held that perfumes lack the creativity required for copyright, in 2006 and 2008 [2].

In the European Union, the Court of Justice ruled in L'Oreal's favor in a 2009 case against Belgian perfume maker Bellure, which had distributed a list comparing its cheaper fragrances to L'Oreal products including Lancome's Tresor. Cosmetics Business reported that the court held a finding of confusion over origin is not required to establish unfair advantage; an intellectual property solicitor quoted in the report said the judgement gave brand owners a way to challenge rivals' commercial advantage [4]. The Fragplace guide states that dupes are legal original formulations because formulas are not patented the way brand names are, and says its warnings concern counterfeit bottles of the originals rather than honestly labeled dupes; it lists poor packaging, missing ingredient lists and little community reputation as warning signs [1].

Fragrance ingredients can irritate skin or trigger allergy in some people. Wikipedia reports that the International Fragrance Association banned Balsam of Peru as a fragrance compound in 1982 and that an EU directive required 26 recognized fragrance allergens to be listed on labels from 11 March 2005, at thresholds of 0.001 percent in leave-on products and 0.01 percent in rinse-off products [2]. The article also notes that some fragrances can trigger asthma in sensitive people [2]. Labeling and ingredient disclosure vary between large houses and small analog makers, and numbered analogs sold informally may not list ingredients [1][2].
No studies found. Research on fragrance allergy and asthma exists for perfumes in general, but no published study has examined numbered analogs specifically [2].

timeline.event: Ernest Beaux prepares numbered sample vials for Chanel, from which No. 5 is chosen [3].
Chanel No. 5 launches on 5 May at the rue Cambon boutique [3].
IFRA bans Balsam of Peru as a fragrance compound [2].
EU rules requiring declaration of 26 fragrance allergens come into force on 11 March [2].
Dutch Supreme Court grants copyright to Lancome's Tresor in Lancome v. Kecofa; French Supreme Court rules against perfume copyright in Bsiri-Barbir v. Haarman & Reimer [2].
French Supreme Court again denies copyright to a perfume in Beaute Prestige International v. Senteur Mazal [2].
European Court of Justice rules for L'Oreal against Bellure over a smell-alike comparison list [4].

lore.intro: Shoppers and buyer's guides discuss analogs and dupes mainly in terms of price, similarity to the original and staying power [1].

claims.claim: An analog smells essentially the same as the designer original.
claims.believers: Dupe guides describe some products as close matches to Baccarat Rouge 540 or Creed Aventus at a fraction of the price [1].
claims.experts: The same guide says almost none smell identical, with differences in the first 15 to 30 minutes, longevity and complexity [1].

claims.claim: Analogs are legal because scents cannot be copyrighted.
claims.believers: Sellers and guides say formulas are not patented the way brand names are, so original formulations are allowed [1].
claims.experts: Wikipedia reports that courts disagree: Dutch and French supreme courts reached opposite conclusions on copyright in perfumes, and the US question is unaddressed [2].

claims.claim: Comparison lists naming the original are harmless.
claims.believers: Smell-alike makers use lists matching their numbers to famous fragrances so buyers know what each smells like [4].
claims.experts: The European Court of Justice held in 2009 that such a list can take unfair advantage of a brand even without confusion [4].

claims.claim: Cheap analogs last as long as the originals.
claims.believers: Some budget options are praised for projection [1].
claims.experts: A retail guide reports 4 to 6 hours for a typical dupe against 8 or more for a luxury original [1].

claims.claim: A very low price means synthetic oil in alcohol.
claims.believers: Guides say bottles near $3 per 100 ml are likely synthetic oil [1].
claims.experts: Wikipedia notes synthetics are more consistent than naturals but not always cheaper, since some have long, low-yield routes [2].

claims.claim: Fragrance can be worn without skin risk.
claims.believers: Dupe buyers treat analogs as ordinary perfume.
claims.experts: Wikipedia reports allergens, asthma triggers and EU labeling rules for 26 allergens [2].
